summary: Psalm 150 closes the Psalter with a rapid summons to praise. It names where praise is offered, why God is praised, the instruments and movement that can join it, and finally widens the call to everything that has breath.
whyItMatters: As the last psalm, it gathers the collection’s long movement of lament, trust, memory, and thanksgiving into a final burst of praise. It does not explain away earlier trouble; it ends by calling all living breath toward God.

context.author: Psalms is an anthology with many writers and collections; this chapter names no individual author.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, and later Jewish and Christian communities that adopted the Psalms for public prayer and private life.
context.date: Individual psalms may come from different periods from the monarchy through the postexilic period; assigning one date to all Psalms would be misleading.
context.setting: Psalm 150 stands at the end of Book V and at the end of the 150-psalm Hebrew Psalter, where the closing psalms begin and end with Hallelujah.
context.literaryForm: Highly compressed Hebrew poetry and public praise, built here almost entirely from repeated imperatives and accumulating lines.

outline.heading: Praise in God’s places
outline.note: The psalm begins by summoning praise in God’s sanctuary and in his heavens.

outline.heading: Praise for who God is and what God does
outline.note: The reason for praise is stated as God’s mighty acts and excellent greatness.

outline.heading: Praise with instruments
outline.note: Trumpet, harp, lyre, tambourine, dancing, strings, flute, and cymbals are gathered into the sound of praise.

outline.heading: Praise from all breath
outline.note: The final line expands the summons to everything that has breath and ends with the same call: Praise Yah.

keyVerses.text: Praise Yah! Praise God in his sanctuary! Praise him in his heavens for his acts of power!
keyVerses.why: This opening sets the chapter’s repeated command and names both God’s sanctuary and a heavenly setting.

keyVerses.text: Praise him for his mighty acts! Praise him according to his excellent greatness!
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the chapter’s stated reasons for praise: what God has done and God’s own greatness.

keyVerses.text: Let everything that has breath praise Yah! Praise Yah!
keyVerses.why: The final verse turns the psalm’s summons outward to every living breather and closes the whole Psalter with praise.

questions.question: What does this chapter actually do?
questions.answer: Psalm 150 is almost entirely a summons to praise. It moves from the place of praise, to the reasons for praise, to the instruments and dancing that accompany praise, and then to everything that has breath.

questions.question: Who is being praised?
questions.answer: The chapter names God and Yah. In the hosted World English Bible, “Yah” is a shortened form used in the praise cry, while “God” is the direct object of praise in the opening line.

questions.question: Where does the psalm say praise happens?
questions.answer: Verse 1 names God’s sanctuary and God’s heavens. The line holds together a worship setting and a cosmic setting without explaining exactly how they relate.

questions.question: Why should God be praised in this psalm?
questions.answer: Verse 2 gives two reasons: God’s mighty acts and God’s excellent greatness. The psalm does not list the acts here, but the wider Psalter repeatedly remembers creation, rescue, judgment, mercy, and care.

questions.question: Why are so many instruments named?
questions.answer: The list makes praise audible and public: trumpet, harp, lyre, tambourine, stringed instruments, flute, and cymbals all appear. The effect is accumulation rather than technical instruction about one required musical arrangement.

questions.question: Does the mention of dancing mean every worship setting must include dance?
questions.answer: The chapter depicts dancing as part of the praise it imagines. Readers differ about how directly ancient worship descriptions should shape later worship practices, but the verse itself presents embodied movement as one fitting form of praise.

questions.question: What is the difference between loud cymbals and resounding cymbals?
questions.answer: Verse 5 repeats cymbals with two descriptions, intensifying the sound. The point is not to define two modern instruments but to heighten the volume and force of the final musical summons.

questions.question: Who is included in “everything that has breath”?
questions.answer: The phrase widens the call beyond one singer or one group. The psalm does not pause to define the boundary, but its language points to all living breath as the fitting responder to Yah.

questions.question: Why does Psalms end this way after so many laments and complaints?
questions.answer: Psalms includes protest, grief, guilt, memory, trust, and praise. Psalm 150 does not erase those earlier voices; as the final chapter of the Hebrew Psalter, it gives the collection a closing direction toward total praise.

glossary.def: The repeated action commanded throughout the chapter: directing honor and celebration to Yah or God.
The place named in verse 1 where God is praised; in Psalms, many poems are oriented toward worship connected with Jerusalem and its temple.
The elevated realm named alongside the sanctuary in verse 1, expanding the setting of praise beyond an earthly place.
The life sign named in verse 6; the closing call includes everything that has breath.
